\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance.} LLM information extraction (prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning) enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, and is attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \citep{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 50.4\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level), near-halving or worse. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, which places them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \citep{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two factors: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Dimension~1 and Dimension~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).

This study combines correlational analyses with quasi-experimental manipulation (BCS-controlled batches) to characterize how schema properties predict extraction accuracy.

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what modes do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To our knowledge, we present the first controlled study isolating type confusability from type count via stratified design in zero-shot LLM IE, spanning NER, RE, and event detection (ED). We quantify confusability using pairwise embedding similarity, the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS), and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We evaluate on Few-NERD \citep{fewnerd-2021}, FewRel \citep{fewrel-2018}, DocRED \citep{docred-2019}, and MAVEN \citep{maven-2020} using Qwen3-32B (\S\ref{sec:experimental_setup}).

Our experiments yield four findings:
(1)~Degradation operates along two dimensions with bounded interaction: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp) and confusability-related type substitution, confirmed on sentence- and document-level RE (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}, \S\ref{sec:multi_channel}).
(2)~Pairwise SCS predicts type confusion across NER, RE, and ED (\S\ref{sec:pairwise}); at batch level, BCS predicts RE accuracy independent of output format (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}) but not NER accuracy; per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}).
(3)~Effects are consistent across schema sizes, prompt designs, and models from three architecture families (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
(4)~Schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification (NER, ED) and routing failure (RE), despite oracle routing recovering substantial accuracy (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).
Several findings are non-obvious: modest pairwise signals ($r^2 {\approx} 1.3\%$) amplify to $R^2 {=}\, 22\text{--}58\%$ at batch level; renaming confusable types \emph{decreases} accuracy (Appendix~\ref{app:renaming}); and few-shot demonstrations widen rather than close the confusability gap.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item We present what is, to our knowledge, the first controlled study that isolates count and confusability effects in training-free LLM extraction. Building on the embedding-similarity criterion from prior schema-partitioning work \citep{llm-pee-2025}, we design stratified experiments that quantify confusability's predictive relationship with extraction degradation across NER, RE, and event detection (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}, \S\ref{sec:pairwise}, \S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
    \item We document a task asymmetry: BCS explains 22--58\% of RE accuracy variance through type substitution---an effect confirmed as format-independent---yet shows no batch-level signal in NER despite significant pairwise effects (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}, \S\ref{sec:multi_channel}).
    \item We identify structural barriers to confusability-aware extraction: schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification (NER, ED) and routing failure (RE), establishing that the decompose-then-merge paradigm faces fundamental precision--recall tradeoffs in training-free IE (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance.} LLM information extraction (prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning) enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, and is attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \citep{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 50.4\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level), near-halving or worse. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, which places them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \citep{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two factors: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Dimension~1 and Dimension~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).

This study combines correlational analyses with quasi-experimental manipulation (BCS-controlled batches) to characterize how schema properties predict extraction accuracy.

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what modes do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To our knowledge, we present the first controlled study isolating type confusability from type count via stratified design in zero-shot LLM IE, spanning NER, RE, and event detection (ED). We quantify confusability using pairwise embedding similarity, the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS), and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We evaluate on Few-NERD \citep{fewnerd-2021}, FewRel \citep{fewrel-2018}, DocRED \citep{docred-2019}, and MAVEN \citep{maven-2020} using Qwen3-32B (\S\ref{sec:experimental_setup}).

Our experiments yield four findings:
(1)~Degradation operates along two dimensions with bounded interaction: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp) and confusability-related type substitution, confirmed on sentence- and document-level RE (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}, \S\ref{sec:multi_channel}).
(2)~Pairwise SCS predicts type confusion across NER, RE, and ED (\S\ref{sec:pairwise}); at batch level, BCS predicts RE accuracy independent of output format (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}) but not NER accuracy; per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}).
(3)~Effects are consistent across schema sizes, prompt designs, and models from three architecture families (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
(4)~Schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification (NER, ED) and routing failure (RE), despite oracle routing recovering substantial accuracy (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).
Several findings are non-obvious: modest pairwise signals ($r^2 {\approx} 1.3\%$) amplify to $R^2 {=}\, 22\text{--}58\%$ at batch level; renaming confusable types \emph{decreases} accuracy (Appendix~\ref{app:renaming}); and few-shot demonstrations widen rather than close the confusability gap.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item We present what is, to our knowledge, the first controlled study that isolates count and confusability effects in training-free LLM extraction. input.new_string:
\paragraph{Equivalence margin justification.}
We set the $\pm 3$\,pp margin based on three converging anchors. \emph{External}: evaluation variance in IE benchmarks typically spans 2--5\,pp across random seeds, prompt variations, and data splits \citep{card-2020-power,dror-2018-significance}; a within-margin interaction would be indistinguishable from routine evaluation noise. \emph{Internal}: $0.5 \times$ within-cell SD ($= 2.3$\,pp) corresponds to Cohen's $d \approx 0.5$ (medium effect threshold; \citealt{lakens-2017-equivalence}), cross-validated against the IQR-predicted confusability main effect of 2.2\,pp (\S\ref{sec:practical_magnitude})---an interaction exceeding 3\,pp would represent ${>}130\%$ amplification. \emph{Sensitivity}: Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity} shows equivalence holds from $\pm 2$\,pp ($p = 0.047$) through $\pm 5$\,pp ($p < 0.001$) on the probability scale; the conclusion is not margin-dependent.

lines: \item \textbf{Effect size and statistical design.} Pairwise SCS explains a small fraction of type confusion variance; entity frequency, prompt position, and mention ambiguity likely account for the remainder. The count $\times$ BCS interaction is bounded on FewRel but nonzero on DocRED, partially confounded by BCS range restriction at higher counts (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}); logit-scale evidence remains inconclusive. DocRED count curves use 5 batches per level due to higher per-batch evaluation cost. BCS-controlled experiments use a single seed with greedy decoding; residual variance is small (Appendix~\ref{app:variance-decomposition}) but precise magnitudes may vary.

-\item \textbf{Task scope.} Format independence is confirmed via paired constrained/unconstrained comparison (Appendix~\ref{app:format-independence}). BCS batch-level prediction is task-dependent: significant in RE but null in NER, where errors scatter across miss, boundary, and type modes rather than concentrating in type substitution. A post-hoc relaxed-matching evaluation confirms that relaxing the span criterion does not recover the BCS signal (Appendix~\ref{app:relaxed-matching}), ruling out evaluation stringency as the explanation.

+\item \textbf{Task scope.} Format independence is confirmed via paired constrained/unconstrained comparison (Appendix~\ref{app:format-independence}). BCS batch-level prediction is task-dependent: significant in RE but null in NER, where errors scatter across miss, boundary, and type modes rather than concentrating in type substitution. A post-hoc relaxed-matching evaluation confirms that relaxing the span criterion does not recover the BCS signal (Appendix~\ref{app:relaxed-matching}), ruling out evaluation stringency as the explanation. The NER batch-level BCS null is confirmed on two models (Qwen3-32B, LLaMA-3.1-8B; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model_ner_null}) but not validated on LLaMA-70B or Gemini; the null could in principle be model-dependent.

\item \textbf{Causal mechanism.} The study establishes correlational evidence with controlled stratification; mechanistic analysis at the attention or logit level is needed to confirm the causal pathway. A post-hoc renaming experiment (Appendix~\ref{app:renaming}) suggests that SCS may proxy deeper conceptual overlap rather than surface label similarity; however, this remains post-hoc and requires more controlled causal analysis.
